challenges.title: Recursion and Dynamic Programming
description: Scientific computing often requires solving complex optimization problems using recursion and dynamic programming (DP). Python excels at expressing these algorithms cleanly.

# Python: Fibonacci with memoization from functools import lru_cache @lru_cache(maxsize=None) def fib(n): if n <= 1: return n return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) fib(50) # extremely fast vs naive recursion
Python's @lru_cache decorator automatically memoizes function results — the equivalent of manually building a cache dictionary. In JavaScript, you implement this with a memo object.

Dynamic programming breaks problems into overlapping subproblems and stores results to avoid redundant computation — essential for computational biology (sequence alignment), ML (Viterbi algorithm), and optimization.
Write a function fibonacci that returns the nth Fibonacci number. It MUST use memoization (a memo object or closure) so that repeated calls are O(1). fibonacci(0) = 0, fibonacci(1) = 1.
tests: assert(fibonacci(1) === 1 && fibonacci(2) === 1, 'message: fibonacci(1) and fibonacci(2) should both return 1.');

challenges.title: Sorting Algorithms: Performance in Data Pipelines
description: Efficient sorting is fundamental to data science — from ranking search results to sorting data before binary search or merge operations. Python's built-in sorted() and .sort() use Timsort (O(n log n) worst case), a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort.

# Python sorting data = [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90] sorted(data) # returns new sorted list data.sort() # in-place sort sorted(data, reverse=True) # descending # Sort objects by key people = [{'name': 'Bob', 'age': 30}, {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}] sorted(people, key=lambda p: p['age']) # [{'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}, ...]
Understanding sort performance matters at scale: sorting 1 million records with O(n²) bubble sort takes ~1 trillion operations vs ~20 million with O(n log n).
Implement merge sort in JavaScript. Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: split the array in half, recursively sort each half, then merge the sorted halves. It runs in O(n log n) time.
challengeSeed: // Merge two sorted arrays into one sorted array
tests: assert(JSON.stringify(mergeSort([64,34,25,12,22,11,90])) === '[11,12,22,25,34,64,90]', 'message: Should correctly sort a longer array.');

challenges.title: Binary Search and Efficient Lookups
description: Binary search is one of the most important algorithms in computer science. It finds a target in a sorted array in O(log n) time by repeatedly halving the search space.

# Python binary search import bisect # Manual implementation def binary_search(arr, target): left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1 while left <= right: mid = (left + right) // 2 if arr[mid] == target: return mid elif arr[mid] < target: left = mid + 1 else: right = mid - 1 return -1 binary_search([1,3,5,7,9,11], 7) # returns 3
In data science, binary search is used to: find thresholds in sorted probability distributions, search sorted database indexes, and implement efficient range queries.
For n=1,000,000 elements: linear search = up to 1,000,000 comparisons; binary search = at most 20 comparisons (log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20).
Implement binarySearch that takes a sorted array arr and a target value. Return the index of target if found, or -1 if not found.
challengeSeed: // Compare arr[mid] with target and update left/right
tests: assert(binarySearch([1,3,5,7,9,11], 4) === -1, 'message: Should return -1 for a missing value.');
